They heard a strange noise coming from the riverbank. It sounded like a woman singing, but they could see no one. Suddenly, a great big sea monster appeared out of the fog. The two young men were terrified and ran for their canoe. They paddled as fast as they could back to Egulac but looked back and saw the monster was still coming towards them. Just as it was about to reach them, they woke up. It was all a dream.

Later that day, the two young men went back to the river to hunt seals. It was foggy and calm again and as they were paddling in the fog, they heard a voice singing. It was a woman's voice. They looked around but could not see anyone. Suddenly, a great big sea monster appeared out of the fog. They were terrified and paddled as fast as they could back to Egulac.

When they got there, they went to the chief and told him what had happened. The chief was a very old man who had lived there all of his life. He told them that a long time ago, there was a very beautiful woman who lived on the other side of the river. Men would often try to capture her but she was a spirit and could not be captured. The only way to appease her was to offer her gifts. The men would give her furs and food but one day they ran out of gifts. That was when the sea monster appeared. It was the woman's spirit in animal form. They needed to give her a gift so the men went down to the river and gave her furs and food. After that, the woman's spirit no longer appeared in that form.

The young men were relieved and happy that they were not going to be eaten by the sea monster. They went back to their homes and told everyone what had happened. From that day on, they respected the woman's spirit and gave her gifts whenever they went to hunt seals.

This story is part of the Tlingit oral tradition.


== References ==

Suddenly they heard a strange noise and then felt the water under them begin to move.  They looked at each other and then looked ahead and saw a great big sea monster rising out of the water toward them.  The two young men were frightened and paddled quickly away toward the safety of the shore.  But no matter how hard they paddled the monster was always right behind them.

Just as they thought all was lost, the fog lifted and the sun came up.  To their relief they saw that the monster was not a monster at all but a huge whale beaching itself on the shore.

The two young men were relieved and grateful to be alive but they never went seal hunting again.  From that day on they became peaceful fishermen.

This story is from the Tlingit tribe of the northwest coast of America.

They continued to hunt and heard the sound again and one of them said, 'That's a human being all right, let's go and find out who it is.' They followed the sound and came to a clearing in the forest where they saw a light. They approached it and saw a woman lying on a bed of leaves. She was weeping and crying and her clothes were torn. The two young men were shocked and frightened and they turned to leave but she called out to them and beckoned them to come closer. They went to her and she spoke to them in a gentle voice, saying, 'You have come to take me away, have come to take me away from this place of suffering.' The two young men looked at each other and then back at the woman and one of them said, 'We have not come to take you away, we have come to take your suffering away.' And they took her home with them to Egulac.

Suddenly they heard a whirring noise and then felt a spray on their faces. They looked around but could see nothing. It happened again and again, the spray getting nearer each time. Finally they saw a huge shape moving towards them in the fog. It was a Steller's sea cow, coming towards them to breathe. The men were terrified and beached the huge creature, probably on the coast of what is now British Columbia. They then killed it with their spears.
The Steller's sea cow was a huge sea cow, growing up to 11 feet long and weighing up to 4 tons. It had grey skin and a small head with small eyes and no external ears. Its eyes were so small that it could not see well on land. It could hold its breath for up to 40 minutes, and could dive to depths of 300 feet. It ate seaweed and the beds of oyster and mussel beds. It had no natural enemies.
The Steller's sea cow was discovered in 1741 by a Russian expedition led by Vitus Bering. They thought it was a type of whale and called it the Sea Cow because of its size and the shape of its head. The sea cow was harmless and slow-moving, but its meat was good to eat and its skin was valuable. Sea otters liked to eat sea cows and the Russians gave the otters to the sailors to eat.
The Russians hunted the sea cow for its meat and skin, and the Americans hunted it for its blubber. The sea cow could not survive this and it became very rare. It was extinct by 1767.

The story of the two young men from Egulac is a traditional story of the Tlingit people. The story is told in several versions, and in some versions the young men are hunting for salmon instead of seals. The story is sometimes told as a creation myth, explaining how the Tlingit people were divided into two groups that lived on opposite sides of Sitka Sound.

Egulac is a village in the Yukon, located at the mouth of the Egulac River on the Yukon River. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: It is now uninhabited, but was the site of the Egulac Trading Post, a major trading post in the late 19th century.
The name Egulac comes from the Gwich'in language and means "the place where we hunt seals".

Geography
Egulac is located at the confluence of the Yukon River and the Egulac River, 12 km (7.5 mi) south of Haines Junction. It is in the traditional territory of the Gwich'in people.

History
The Egulac Trading Post was first established in 1898 by the Canadian government as a supply post for the Yukon River steamers. In 1900, the post was taken over by the North West Trading Company. The post was an important supply point for miners in the Klondike Gold Rush. The post closed in 1917.
The Egulac Trading Post was operated by the Hudson's Bay Company from 1942 to 1957.

They lived there in peace for many years but then a great plague came upon them. The Tlingit call the plague "shaash-ka-la-shoot," which means "the sickness that makes you crazy." The people who fell sick with this plague would cry all the time, and sometimes they would kill their own children. The Tlingit say that the woman in the water is one of the spirits of this plague. She cries because she has been separated from her child, who was taken from her by the plague.

The story of the woman in the water was recorded by Frances Densmore in 1916.

The story
The story begins with two young men from Egulac going down to the river to hunt seals. It becomes foggy and calm and they hear a strange noise coming from the riverbank. One of the young men suggests that it is a bear, but the other is sure that it is a human. They argue about this until they decide to investigate. They go towards the noise and see two figures standing on the bank. As they get closer, they see that the two figures are Kwakiutl Indians, one wearing a cedar bark helmet and the other a cedar bark dress. The young men are terrified and run back to their canoe and row back to Egulac as fast as they can. They tell their friends and family what had happened and they decide to move to a new village site, because they thought that the Indians were evil spirits.

The tale is unusual in that the Indians are portrayed as evil spirits. It is possible that the story is a version of the "evil magician" tale type, but with the roles of the humans and supernatural beings reversed. It is also possible that the tale is a version of the "dream interpreter" tale type, but with the roles of the humans and supernatural beings also reversed. The tale may have been told to explain why the Kwakiutl were not living at the old village site at Egulac.

The Kwakiutl people were a confederation of tribes of the northwest coast of North America, from Cape Mudge on the west coast of Vancouver Island to the mouth of the Skeena River. They spoke a Wakashan language.
Their economy was based on the resources of the sea. They hunted sea mammals such as seals, sea lions, whales and porpoises. They also fished for salmon, halibut, rockfish and lingcod. They gathered shellfish such as clams, mussels, and sea urchins.
Their population was about 3,000 in 1778. They lived in longhouses of up to 100 feet (30 m) in length. Each longhouse could hold up to 300 people. They had a highly developed culture, and were known for their wood carvings, including totem poles.
In 1828 the Kwakiutl were visited by George Vancouver III, the great-nephew of Captain George Vancouver. He made detailed sketches of their houses, carvings, and ceremonies.
In 1850 the Kwakiutl were visited by Edward S. Curtis, who was to become one of their most famous photographers.
In 1871 the Kwakiutl were visited by Franz Boas, who was to become their most famous anthropologist.

The harbinger of death
A harbinger of death is a creature from the folklore of the Tlingit and Haida peoples of the northwestern Pacific coasts of Canada and America. It is described as a large, white, sea-going creature, resembling a cross between a killer whale and a walrus. It has a human face with flared nostrils, and red eyes. It is said to be a harbinger of death because when it appears, it is said to be a sign that a tribe's most important elder or leader is about to die.

Background
The St. John's Day Boat Regatta is an annual boat race on the northwest coast of Newfoundland that takes place on the closest Saturday to St. John's Day (24 June) in the waters off the Gros Morne National Park. The regatta is one of the oldest sporting events in North America and is considered one of the most colourful and exciting events in all of Newfoundland. The first recorded race was in 1823.
The race is run in two divisions: the "oar" boats, which are propelled only by human effort, and the "engine" boats, which have auxiliary engines in addition to sails. The course is approximately 18 miles (29 km) long and runs from the "Sandy Cove" start line to the finish line at "Bull Arm".
The regatta is a very important part of the culture of the area and is a source of great pride for the residents of the area. Many families have built beautiful handcrafted wooden boats for the race. These boats are not just raced, but are often sailed to the start line from as far away as Woody Point.
The regatta has inspired at least one piece of music. "The Boat Race" is a reel that is often played at Celtic music sessions.

The Ogopogo is a large lake monster that is said to inhabit the waters of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. Egulac
Egulac is an abandoned Tlingit village located on a bluff overlooking the Dixon Entrance, across from the city of Prince Rupert, British Columbia. The name Egulac comes from the Tlingit word "Ega" meaning "bald eagle" and "clac" meaning "place". The village was a small fishing and hunting village. In 1900, there were 160 residents. The population declined as the Tlingit people were forced to leave their traditional territories and move to the city of Prince Rupert. Today, the Tlingit people continue to fish in the area and use the Egulac fishing lodge.

The people of the Egulac village were hunters and gatherers of the indigenous First Peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast of Canada and the United States. They were part of the Tlingit and Haida Nations. The Egulac people lived in a large extended family group and were governed by a chief and a council of elders. They hunted sea otter, sea lion, seal, deer, bear, and mountain goat. They also fished for salmon, halibut, and rockfish. They gathered clams, oysters, mussels, berries, and seaweed.
Their population was estimated to be between 400 and 500 people in the early 1800s. The Egulac people lived in plank houses on piles above the tidal marsh at the mouth of the Tongass Narrows, which is between the islands of Admiralty and Kupreanof in the Alexander Archipelago of Southeast Alaska.
Their traditional territory was the central and northern part of the Tongass Narrows, including the islands of Taku, Angoon, and Kupreanof. The people of Egulac were part of the Taku Group, which included the people of the Taku River, Guna, and Sitka.
The Egulac people were the last residents of Egulac village. The other villages in the Egulac territory were abandoned much earlier. The people moved to Sitka, Hoonah, and Angoon.

The Okanagan people believe that they were created by a Supreme Being. They believe that the Supreme Being made them out of the dirt of the earth and breathed the breath of life into them. They believe that the Supreme Being gave them their language, their culture, and their history. They believe that the Supreme Being made the world and everything in it, but that he let them have free will. They believe that the Supreme Being watches over them and helps them when they need it.

The Okanagan people believe that there are many spirits in the world. They believe that there are spirits of the land, the water, the animals, and the plants. They believe that these spirits can help or hurt people, depending on how people behave. They believe that people should respect the spirits and take care of the world that the Supreme Being gave them.

Suddenly they heard a whirring noise near the water's edge, and as the fog lifted they saw a pair of large eyes looking at them. It was the eyes of a great white shark. The two men were terrified and ran as fast as they could back to Egulac. From that day on they never went down to the river to hunt seals again.

The story
The story of the two young men from Egulac and the great white shark is a traditional tale of the Tlingit people. It is told to explain why the Tlingit people do not eat shark meat, even though it is a valuable source of food for other coastal Native American tribes.
The story is told as a cautionary tale. The two young men disrespected the power of the sea and the animals in it by hunting seals at night when they are most active. The shark is a guardian of the sea and punishes the men for their disrespect.
The story is also told to explain an unusual feature of Tlingit culture. Tlingit people do not eat shark meat, and will only take the blubber and intestines. This is because the shark took the lives of the two young men.

Geography
The Quatsino River (also spelled Quatsina) is a river on the west coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia. The river is approximately 13 km from the Pacific Ocean, and is a tributary of Nootka Sound. The Quatsino is one of the few rivers on the west coast of Vancouver Island that flows in a southerly direction.
The mouth of the Quatsino River is located south of the village of Quatsino. The river flows through the Quatsino First Nation reserve land and the west side of the Bedwell-Harbour Regional District, and the east side of the Tlatlasikwala First Nation reserve land.
The river is a popular salmon and steelhead fishing destination.

Quatsino people
The Quatsino people have lived in the Quatsino River area for thousands of years. The Quatsino people are one of the Tlingit-speaking groups. According to their oral history, the Quatsino people originally lived in the Taku River area in northern British Columbia. They moved south due to war with other tribes and now occupy reserve land along the northwest coast of Vancouver Island.

They heard a strange noise coming from the riverbank. It was a sound they had never heard before. Suddenly, a large creature emerged from the fog. It was a selkie, an animal that could change its shape into a seal or a human being. The selkie looked at the two young men and then spoke to them in a human voice.

'What are you two doing here?' he asked.

'We have come to hunt seals,' they replied.

'You have no right to hunt my people,' the selkie said angrily. 'We are the children of the water, the rulers of the sea. You have no weapons that can harm us.'

The two young men were afraid and begged the selkie's forgiveness. The selkie thought for a moment and then said, 'I will make a deal with you. I will give you three things that will help you in your lives. But you must promise me that you will never hunt seals again.'

The two young men agreed and the selkie gave them three things: a bag of gold, a bag of precious stones, and a girl who was as beautiful as the morning sun.

The two young men returned home rich and happy, but they kept their promise and never hunted seals again. And the selkie kept his side of the bargain too. He always helped the young men when they were in trouble and they lived long and prosperous lives.

This story is a good reminder that we should always be kind to animals and respect the world around us. The selkie teaches us that we should be careful what we hunt and what we take from the natural world.

Suddenly they heard a loud noise, like a great wave crushing the shore. Then they heard war cries, and then gun fire.
The two young men ran for the hills and hid. When the fog lifted the next morning, they saw that the German warship SMS Emder U-Boot was stranded high and dry on the shore. The warship was a total loss.

The Emder U-Boot
The Emder U-Boot was one of three German warships that were being built as commerce raiders during World War I. The other two were the Seydlitz and the Brummer. They were designed to be fast and large submarines, with a displacement of 1,300 tons and a speed of 17 knots. They were armed with four 105 mm guns and six torpedo tubes. The submarines were 105 metres long and had a crew of 70.
The Emder U-Boot was launched on 1 June 1917, and commissioned on 24 August. On 21 October, the submarine left Wilhelmshaven for a mission to attack British shipping in the North Atlantic.
On 28 October, the submarine was in the St. Lawrence River, looking for a target, when it hit a mine and began to sink. The crew abandoned ship, and the submarine sank at 6:15 am. The crew was picked up by a Canadian fisherman, and taken to Rimouski.

Aftermath
The stranding of the Emder U-Boot was a propaganda coup for the British, and the incident was widely reported in the Canadian press. The crew was detained as prisoners of war, and eventually sent to Toronto as an "Honoured Guest" to the Canadian National Exhibition in 1918.
The wreck of the Emder U-Boot is a popular dive site. The submarine is partially buried in sand and rocks, and the hull is broken in two.

Egulac
Egulac is an extremely remote reserve located on a high bluff overlooking the Queen Charlotte Sound, on the west coast of Vancouver Island, about 30 km north of Tofino. It is the home reserve of the Owekeeno (also spelled "Owecan" or "Oh-WEE-kay-noh") people. The reserve has an area of 1,584 hectares (15.84 km2).
The reserve is very isolated. The only way to get there is by boat or a very long hike. There is no cell phone coverage. The reserve has its own search and rescue team.

Fishing
Fishing is an important part of the culture of the Owekeeno people. The Tla-o-qui-aht and the Owekeeno have a treaty fishing right that allows them to fish for salmon and bottom fish in the same areas as the commercial fishermen, but before the commercial fishermen are allowed to fish. The First Nations people can also catch unlimited amount of fish for their personal use, for ceremonial purposes and for their potlatch.

Tourism
The reserve has a band office, band hall, daycare, small store, clinic, and a small park. There is a water taxi that takes people to the reserve. The Owekeeno people depend a lot on tourism. The Owekeeno people have a beautiful beach and a mountain that is a popular destination for tourists. The Owekeeno people have a campground with 19 sites and a picnic area. The campground is open from May long weekend to October long weekend.
The Owekeeno people have a small museum in the band hall. The museum has a lot of interesting artifacts.

They heard a strange noise and one of them said it was a new kind of locomotive. The other said it was a new kind of spirit. They argued about it and finally decided to find out by feeling their way along the shore. They soon came upon a large bay filled with seals and there they saw a locomotive pulling a train of cars along the beach. The men were astonished and watched as the locomotive came toward them. It stopped just long enough to let the men climb aboard, and then it went on its way down the shoreline.

For many years the people of Egulac had been complaining about the long, long trains that were always getting in the way of their hunting. The railway company had promised to find a way around the Egulac Peninsula, but they had not done so and the Indians were very angry. Now, with the new locomotive running on the beach, the Indians knew they had to act fast. They went to the railway company and demanded that the new route be built. The company promised to do it as soon as the seals left the beach.

The Indians decided to scare the seals away. They got some old rags and soaked them in seal oil. Then they set the rags on fire and scattered them along the beach. The seals panicked and swam out to sea. The Indians watched as the new locomotive came along the beach and then went inland to build the new route.

This story is often told as a tale of the ingenuity of the native people, but in reality it is a tale of their destruction. The burning of the seal oil spilled into the ocean killed all the baby seals and many of the adults. The seal population never fully recovered and even today is still not what it was before the incident.

The Egulac Seal Oil Spill is considered to be the first major environmental disaster in Canada.

Then they heard a voice calling them. It was the voice of the Raven, calling from the river bank. The Raven spoke of a great treasure that was hidden nearby, but warned the young men that they would not be able to share it with anyone. The young men agreed to the condition, and the Raven revealed the location of the treasure. The two men went to the spot and found a great pile of copper and silver. The two young men returned to their people empty-handed, but with a story to tell.

Variants
This story is told with variations by many Northwest Coast tribes. In some versions, the treasure is gold and silver, in others it is copper. In some versions, the treasure is cursed because the men spoke of it to others, in others it is cursed because the men tried to divide it unequally. In some versions, the men are brothers, in others they are strangers who meet on the river bank.

Finally, a young boy named Tula grew up with the knowledge of the whale and learned how to communicate with it. He learned that the whale was not coming to hurt them, but to play. Tula learned the clicks and whistles of the killer whale and then taught these sounds to the other Egulac people.

With this new knowledge the Egulac people were able to live in peace with the killer whale. They learned that the whale did not mean to harm them and that they could live together in the same area. The Egulac people became the only people in the world who could communicate with the killer whale. They became very proud of this and told stories of Tula for many years.

The young men agreed, and they lived in the city for many years, helping the dream people whenever they could.

Eventually the two young men grew old and died, but their spirits stayed in the city. Some say that if you go down to the river on a calm and foggy night, you can see the City of Broughton and the two old men who live there, helping the dream people.

Geography
The City of Broughton is a Dreamtime site in the Yukon, located at the confluence of the Broughton River and the Yukon River. Today, there is no permanent settlement at this location, but it is an important site for the local First Nations people.
The site is a National Historic Site of Canada, and is managed by Parks Canada. It is an important archaeological site, and is the location of the oldest known Tlingit house posts in the Yukon.

The story
The story is told by the Tlingit narrator, who says:

Once upon a time, two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals. It was getting dark when they heard a strange noise coming from the water. One of them said, "What is that?" The other answered, "It's a new kind of seal." "No, it's a new kind of bird," said the other. They argued about it until they decided to find out what it was. They shot at it with their pistols and found that it was a seal. The next day they went back to the place where they had heard the noise and found a new kind of bird.

Analysis
The story is a classic example of a "new kind" story, a genre that is common in Native American folklore. The genre is characterized by the phrase "new kind of," and the stories often involve the discovery of something previously unknown. In this story, the two young men are unable to identify a sound they hear on the water, and when they investigate, they discover a new kind of seal. The next day, they find a new kind of bird. The story is a reminder that even in a familiar environment, there are always new things to discover.

The Whale's Cry
The Whale's Cry is a story told by the Tlingit people. A long time ago, a young Tlingit boy named Aan was out on the water hunting for seals with his older brother. It was a calm, foggy night. They had just set their net when they heard a strange sound. It was a cry, a wail, coming from the darkness. It was a cry of a mother whale mourning for her calf that had been taken by a killer whale. Aan and his brother were so scared they ran away, back to their village. They never spoke of this experience again.

Aan's sister, Tla-lah, was worried. Her brother had been gone for a long time and had not returned. She went to look for him. She followed the sound of the wail and came upon the mother whale. She was weeping for her calf. Tla-lah tried to comfort the whale, but the mother only cried louder. Tla-lah stayed with the whale all night, comforting her. The next day Tla-lah led her brother's body back to the village.
Aan's death was a great loss to the Tlingit people. They held a big potlatch to honor Aan and to thank Tla-lah for bringing his body back. Tla-lah received many gifts for her bravery.

The Whale's Cry and the Tlingit People
The Tlingit people have a deep respect for the natural world. They believe that everything in the world is connected, including humans, animals, and spirits. The Whale's Cry is a reminder of the interconnectedness of all things. It is also a story of bravery, of how Tla-lah bravely faced the mother whale and stayed with her all night. The story is still told today, passed down from generation to generation.

The next day the Chilkat came down to the same place to hunt seals and found their dead. They went back up to their village to gather warriors.

A great battle took place between the Tlingit warriors and the Egulac warriors. The Egulac warriors were good fighters and they had the advantage of fighting on their own territory. The Tlingits were almost wiped out. Only a few young braves escaped.

The Tlingits went to the Klondike gold fields and joined up with their relatives and kinsmen. They became miners and found gold. They sent for their women and children to come and join them.

Some time later the Egulac people were out hunting when they were attacked by a large party of Tlingit warriors. The Egulac people fought bravely but they were no match for the Tlingits. They were all killed. The Tlingits took their canoes and paddled away to their village.

This battle was part of the feud between the Tlingits and the Egulac people that lasted for many years. It was a very bitter feud.

They decide that they should avoid any further encounters, but they are not sure that they have made the right decision.

The story is a classic example of a tale about the supernatural. It is a common theme in many Native American cultures, and it is often used to explain natural phenomena or to teach moral lessons. In this particular story, the narrator is uncertain about the wisdom of his decision, and that uncertainty is a common theme in many stories of this type.

There are many versions of this story, and it is often told in different ways. Some versions make it clear that the people in the other world are not to be trusted, while others suggest that they are wise and powerful beings who can help the narrator if he is in need. Whirlpools happen when a body of water is spun around its own axis. This can happen when water goes down a drain, or when water is hit by a spinning object. The water in a whirlpool moves very fast. It moves in a circle and pulls anything that comes near it into the middle. The middle of the whirlpool is called the eye. The water in the eye is quiet because it is going round and round so fast that it doesn't have any energy left to make waves.

The Bay of Fundy
The Bay of Fundy is the world's highest tides bay. The tides can be as much as 50 feet. The bay is divided into two parts by a narrow isthmus at Digby, Nova Scotia. The two parts are called the Minas Basin and the Fundy Basin. The Minas Basin is a large part of the Bay of Fundy that is sheltered by Nova Scotia. The Fundy Basin is open to the Atlantic Ocean. The two parts are connected by the 5 mile long and 1 mile wide Passamaquoddy Bay.
The Bay of Fundy is known for its extreme tides. The tides are so high that they are classified as tidal waves. The tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and sun. At spring tides the high tides are higher and the low tides are lower. During neap tides the difference between high and low tide is less. The tides travel up and down the bay at a speed of 20 miles an hour.

Then they heard a loud noise and saw a great light, and when it was close to them, they saw it was an aircraft, and they knew it was the work of humans.

The pilot was flying a Consolidated PBY Catalina flying boat, a Canadian-built amphibian aircraft that had taken off from RCAF Station Patricia Bay, near Victoria, British Columbia, destined for RCAF Station Comox, on Vancouver Island. The pilot was F/L Thomas D. Boulton, RCAF, and his crew were F/O Robert J. Andrews, RCAF, and A.B. John C. Thompson, RCAF. The aircraft was on a cross-country flight training mission.
The pilot had been following the south shore of the Strait of Georgia when a fuel leak caused a fire. The pilot attempted to extinguish the fire but was unable to do so and was forced to make an emergency landing.
The two young men ran to the aircraft and found the crew had abandoned ship. They attempted to extinguish the fire again, but it was too intense. Soon the aircraft was completely engulfed in flames and destroyed.
The crew had bailed out, but F/O Robert J. Andrews was unable to escape the aircraft and was killed in the crash.
The wreck of the aircraft was later found upside down in the sand about 10 metres (33 feet) from the high water mark on the south shore of Cormorant Island in the Discovery Islands.

Aftermath
The wreckage of the aircraft remained on Cormorant Island until 1957 when the Canadian government offered to return it to the families of the crew. The wreckage was removed and taken to Victoria, British Columbia, where it was reassembled and placed on display at the Patricia Bay Museum.
In 1994 the Canadian Forces disposed of the Catalina's remains by burning the wreckage.

The submarine
The submarine was a T-90S Whiskey-class submarine. It was launched in 1937 and was one of the most modern submarines in the world at the time. It had a crew of 52 men. It was 92.5 metres long and had a 6.4 metre diameter pressure hull. It could dive to a depth of 120 metres. It was armed with 10 torpedo tubes and could carry 24 torpedoes. It was powered by two diesel engines and two electric engines. It could cruise at a speed of 16 knots on the surface and 21 knots underwater.

The hunt
The Canadians were worried that the submarine might attack their ships so they decided to hunt it down. They sent out a ship to follow the submarine and to try to find out where it was heading. They also sent out a plane to drop depth charges in front of the submarine. The submarine's crew tried to escape but the Canadians were too fast. They dropped a depth charge directly on top of the submarine and it was damaged. The Canadians then captured the submarine and towed it back to Victoria, British Columbia.

The aftermath
The Canadians were very proud of their victory. They had shown that they were good at hunting submarines. But the other Allied powers were not happy. They accused the Canadians of damaging an important Russian warship. The Russians were also not happy. They demanded that the submarine be returned to them. But the Canadians had no intention of giving it back. They had already stripped the submarine of its best parts and scuttled it.

A spirit came across the water and spoke to them. It warned them that a great storm was coming that would destroy their village. The spirit, governed by the natural world, was unable to help the villagers directly, but it gave them a warning so they could prepare for the coming storm.

The story
According to the legend, two young men from Egulac (a village on the southwest coast of B.C.) went down to the river to hunt seals. They took their canoe out onto the wide expanse of the Broughton Archipelago. It was a calm, still night. The moon was full and the sky was clear of clouds. Suddenly the weather changed. The sky grew dark and a heavy fog settled over the water. In the stillness, the men could hear the spirits speaking.
A spirit came across the water. It spoke to the hunters, warning them that a great storm was coming that would destroy their village. The spirit, governed by the natural world, was unable to help the villagers directly. But the spirit gave them a warning so they could prepare for the coming storm.
The young men paddled back to Egulac and told the other villagers about the storm that was coming. The villagers prepared for the storm by gathering firewood, securing their homes and canoes, and making sure they had enough food.
The next day, a southerly wind began to blow. It grew stronger and soon turned into a fierce wind from the north. A great storm had come, just as the spirit had warned. The storm lasted for days. The villagers stayed inside, keeping warm by the fire. They watched as the wind and rain destroyed their homes and their fields. When the storm finally passed, the villagers went out to survey the damage. They were amazed to find that their homes and fields had been untouched by the storm. The villagers knew that the spirits had protected them.

Variations
There is a similar story from the Tlingit people of the north Pacific. In this story, a raven warns a village of an incoming tsunami.

Geography
The Tlingit people are the original people of the Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska. They have lived there for thousands of years, living off the land and the sea. The Tongass National Forest is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of the islands and the mainland along the coast of southeastern Alaska. The Tlingit people lived in longhouses on the land near the water. They hunted and fished for their food. They traded with other tribes in the area.
The Egulac River is a short river that flows into the southern part of the Tongass National Forest. It is located between Frederick Sound and the Tongass Narrows. The river is about 15 miles (25 km) long. The river flows through a wide valley. The valley is flat near the mouth of the river, but it becomes quite mountainous in the upper part of the valley. The river is very shallow, but it has some rapids and waterfalls. The river is not very deep, but it is wide. It is wide enough that salmon can swim up it to spawn.The Egulac River flows into the Frederick Sound. The Frederick Sound is a long and narrow sound. It connects the Tongass Narrows to the open sea. The sound is about 25 miles (40 km) long. The sound is a very busy waterway. There are many small islands in the sound. The sound is very deep. It is deep enough that large ships can sail into the sound and then go up the Tongass Narrows to Juneau.

The river was so still that it seemed to be 'standing still'. They heard a strange noise and saw a big creature approaching them. It was a Steller's sea cow (Hydromalis stellarum).

Biology
The Steller's sea cow was a large marine mammal, growing to a length of 21 feet (6.4 m) and a weight of 12 tons (11 t). It had a long, narrow snout, small eyes, and small, triangular flippers. It was a herbivore, feeding on seaweed and underwater plants. The Steller's sea cow lived in the shallow, sheltered waters of the North Pacific Ocean, around the coasts of Alaska, Russia, and Japan.
The Steller's sea cow was a relatively new species, having evolved around 14 million years ago. It was closely related to the modern-day manatee.

Extinction
The Steller's sea cow was hunted by humans for its meat and blubber. The large population of sea cows around the Kamchatka Peninsula were hunted to extinction by the mid-18th century. The sea cows of the Commander Islands were hunted out by 1768. The sea cow population in the southern Kuril Islands were also hunted to extinction, but around 1845, a new population appeared, possibly from sea cows that had been stranded on land and survived in a freshwater lake. This population was hunted until 1875, when the Russian government passed a law protecting sea cows. Despite this law, the sea cow population was hunted out again, this time to extinction. The Steller's sea cow was last seen in the wild in 1793.

Suddenly they heard a strange noise and then saw a large sea monster surfacing with a frightening roar. It was a monster of such immense size and shape that the bravest of men would have trembled in fear. The men saw that it had a head like a turtle, a back like a buffalo, a front like a caribou, and its sides were like a salmon swimming upstream. It had eyes like the stars of the night sky, and on its back were raised bumps like the humps of a porcupine.

The two young men were terrified and hid in a nearby cave. They could hear the monster roaring and thrashing about in the water, but it didn't seem to notice them. They stayed there until the monster had finished roaring and left.

The next day they went back to the place where they had seen the monster but there was no sign of the monster, only a few scales and some slime. The two young men went back to their village and told everyone they had seen a monster but no one believed them.

A few days later, two other young men went down to the river to hunt seals and they also saw the monster. This time there were four men who went back to the village to tell what had happened. But the old people didn't believe them either.

This went on for some time and the young men were making fun of the two young men who had first seen the monster. But one day, while the whole village was out hunting, a strange thing happened. A strange noise came up from the river and then the monster appeared. Everyone saw it. It was so frightening that the men ran away. The monster didn't hurt them, but it made them understand that they had to respect the river and the creatures in it. From then on, the people of Egulac lived in peace with the creatures of the river.

The story of the monster is a myth that has been passed down from generation to generation among the Tlingit people of the Yukon. It is a story that reminds the Tlingit people of the power of nature and the importance of respecting all living things.

The story
The story of the Yehl comes from the Tli-gwich'in people of the Yukon. It is a story of two young men who go down to the river to hunt seals. It is a time of fog and calm. The young men hear a strange noise and one of them identifies it as a new kind of animal never before heard. The other says it is the wind among the trees. They go to investigate and find a new kind of animal, the Tli-gwich'in call it the "Yehl".

The Yehl
The Yehl is a type of water shrew. It is semi-aquatic and spends most of its life in or near water. It is a small rodent, about 13 to 15 centimetres long. It has webbed hind feet and fur that is thick and waterproof. It eats seeds, fruits, and aquatic invertebrates. It is a prey animal for many predators.

The story of the Yehl
The Tli-gwich'in people have a story about how the Yehl came to be. In the story two young men are out hunting seals. The weather is foggy and calm. They hear a strange noise and one of them says it is a new kind of animal. The other says it is the wind in the trees. They go to investigate and find a new kind of animal. They try to keep it in a trap but it chews through that too. In the end they set it free. After that they see the Yehl everywhere they go.

Suddenly they heard a voice calling from the water, "Help! Help!"
"Who are you?" one of the young men called out.
"I am the Wind," the voice replied.
"What do you want?" they asked.
"I have blown many a man off the mountain tops, and I have frozen many a river. I have made many a tempest and I have cooled many a hot day. But I am tired. I cannot do it any more. Who will take my place?"
The two young men looked at each other and then back at the river. They were afraid. "We will take your place," they said.
So the Wind was happy and left them there on the river. From that day on, the young men from Egulac lived by the river and when the wind did not blow, they made it blow. When the sun was too hot, they made it cool. And the Wind was happy.

Variations
This story is told by many nations of the Pacific Northwest. In one variation, the two young men are supernaturally gifted with the power to control the weather. In another, it is the Wind who asks them to take his wife, not his job. In still another, it is the two young men who are in love with the Wind's wife, the Sun. In a fourth variation, the two young men are tricked by the Wind into taking his place, only to find out that he was a very unpleasant character indeed.

Raven's Ghost
The Raven's Ghost is a creature of the night in the Haida mythology. It is a spirit that appears when humans disturb the Ravens' nest. The Raven's Ghost is a harbinger of death. When it appears, death is sure to follow. The Raven's Ghost is a large sea monster with red eyes, white fur and slime covering its body. It has a row of sharp teeth and it lets out a blood curdling scream when it appears.

They tried to communicate with the people but no one could understand them.  After some time, they managed to find someone who spoke their language.  It was an old woman who had been a student in Egulac many years before.  She took the two young men under her wing and showed them around the city.

The young men were amazed and amused by almost everything they saw.  They visited a large library and a museum, and they watched television and movies.  They learned that the city was called Vancouver and that it was part of a country called Canada.  They also learned that the strange disease that had killed their families and friends was called smallpox and that it had been brought to Egulac by a careless sailor. The young men spent many days exploring the city and learning about the new world that had arisen since their departure.  They were particularly fascinated by the many different kinds of food available.  They ate at restaurants that served Chinese, Indian, Greek, Mexican, and many other kinds of food.  They also learned that Canada had many different kinds of people living in it, who were descended from people from many different countries.

Finally, the young men were ready to return home.  The old woman took them to the airport and helped them board a plane that would take them back to Egulac.  As they were waiting to board, they saw a newspaper with a front-page story about the discovery of a cure for smallpox.  They were filled with sadness as they thought of the friends and family they had lost.  But they were also filled with hope for the future.  They knew that their lives would never be the same, and that they would always be outsiders in their own land.  But they also knew that they had a new understanding of the world and of the people who lived in it.  And they knew that they would use that understanding to make things better for their people.

In 1873, the Canadian government sent George Mercer Dawson to survey the Yukon. He and his men were based at Egulac (also spelled as Egulagh, Egulach, and Egulukh), on the southern shore of the Yukon River, for the summer. In the winter of 1873–1874, two young men from the nearby native village of Egulac went out on the ice of the Yukon River to hunt seals. It was a foggy and calm night and they heard a strange noise and then saw two glowing lights approaching them. They were afraid and hid. The lights came closer and then stopped. A voice called out and asked them what time it was. They said they did not know. The voice said it was ten o'clock. The men were frightened and hid their faces. The voice asked them again and they again said they did not know. The voice then said it was a good thing they didn't know because at that hour the spirits of the dead come out to hunt for people. The men ran back to Egulac and told their fellow villagers what had happened. The elders among them said that this was the place where the spirits came from and that the people should move their village. So, the villagers moved their houses about 100 metres to the east and rebuilt them. The strange lights were seen again

Suddenly they heard a strange noise and then felt the water under them moving in a strange way. They paddled to the shore and looked for a cause but could find nothing. The fog lifted a little and they saw the strange sight of two seals, one on each side of their canoe, lifting it up out of the water. The story of the two young men from Egulac and their encounter with supernatural beings is a traditional tale of the Tlingit people. It is a version of a more general story type told by many North American indigenous peoples, in which people have an encounter with a creature or creatures that can transform or shape-shift, usually into a dangerous animal such as a bear or a killer whale.

So the two young men agreed to paddle the Great Bear's canoe whenever he needed it. From that day on, the Great Bear took the two young men back to their people whenever they got lost in the fog. They heard a strange noise coming from the river and it was getting closer and closer. It turned out to be a sea monster. The monster had a head like a turtle, a body like a whale, and it had two long horns. It was a female and she had just come ashore to lay her eggs. The two young men were terrified and ran away as fast as they could. They told everyone about the monster and soon the whole village was there to see it. The monster did not hurt them. She let them come close and touch the eggs. The villagers were very happy and grateful. After that, the monster never bothered them again.

Variants
There are many variations of this story. Sometimes it is a young woman who encounters the monster, sometimes it is a group of men who are turned to stone, and sometimes the monster is not a sea monster at all but a giant octopus.

For a long time the Haida did not hunt sea otters because they were not sure they were good to eat. Then they tasted the meat and discovered it was very good. They hunted them to near extinction.

The Haida storyteller then went on to relate how the Haida were once visited by a great white spirit bear. The Haida were warned that they must not hunt this spirit bear or they would lose their land and their people would be sickened with diseases. The Haida were told that they could only hunt the spirit bear in dreams. One man dreamed he was hunting a spirit bear. He was warned in the dream not to touch the bear but to watch it carefully. The man awoke and went to the place in the dream and there he found the spirit bear. He was about to shoot it when the bear spoke to him. The bear told the man that he had been chosen to be the guardian of the spirit bear. The man was told to protect the bear and the land and the Haida people would prosper. The man took this responsibility very seriously. He protected the spirit bear and the land. The Haida people prospered. The man had many descendants. They became the hereditary chiefs of the Haida.

The Haida people have a deep respect for the natural world. They have a saying: "We do not own the land. The land owns us." They have a responsibility to protect the natural world. They have been fighting for years to protect their land from logging. They have a deep respect for the animals and the spirits of the animals. They have a saying: "We are all related." They believe that the actions of one affect all.

They heard a strange noise and one of them said it was an 'ogopogo'. Their cousin who was with them said that it was only a beaver. They argued about this for some time, and then they heard the noise again, and this time they saw a huge shape moving in the water. They saw the 'ogopogo's' head and neck rising out of the water. They were very frightened and ran away as fast as they could.

For many years afterwards, people in the Egulac district reported seeing the 'ogopogo' in the Arrow Lakes.
The Ogopogo is a lake monster of Okanagan legend. It is said to inhabit the waters of the southern end of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia, Canada. The name comes from a mispronunciation of Ogopogo, the proper pronunciation of which is "Oh-go-pogo", after the Okanagan word for "mountain lake".

Description
The Ogopogo is described as being about 30 feet (9.1 m) long and 5 feet (1.5 m) wide, with a green scaly back and a white underbelly. It is said to have a long neck and a small head, and to move gracefully through the water. It is said to be a peaceful creature that rarely troubled humans, although there are a few reports of people being accidentally struck by its fins.

History
The Ogopogo legend is a relatively recent one, having originated some time in the 19th century. There are no reports of the Ogopogo in the earliest European accounts of the lake. The first reports of the creature come from Native Americans, who said that the Ogopogo had been there for as long as they could remember. The first European reports of the Ogopogo come from the Oblate missionaries of St. Joseph's Mission, who first heard the stories from the Native Americans.
The Ogopogo was first seen by a European is believed to be George Frankland, an officer with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who saw the monster in 1872. Since then, many people have reported seeing the Ogopogo, including members of the police, loggers, fishermen, and tourists.

Geography
The reserve is located on the west side of Island Lake, a large lake with many islands, in the Kenora District of Ontario. The geography of the reserve is quite varied. In the north, the reserve is made up of a series of low hills. In the south, the reserve is located on the shores of Island Lake and the water comes right up to the edge of the reserve. The reserve is surrounded on three sides by the Kenora District, and on the fourth side by the Wauzhushk Onigum First Nation reserve.

Demographics
According to the 2021 Canadian census, the Egulac First Nation had a population of 224 living in 100 of its 125 total dwellings, a change of -1.7% from its 2016 population of 228.  With a land area of 2,100.51 km2, it had a population density of 0.11/km2 in 2021.

Then the old man vanished. He left them alone in the fog on the river, and they started for home, paddling hard, trying to outrun the fear that was in them.

They went inland and told the people what had happened. They were not believed. They were ridiculed and called foolish. But the young men knew the truth. They knew that something was going to happen that would change their lives forever.

They decided to go to the Great Trees of the West, even though it meant leaving their own people. They went alone, for no one would go with them. They paddled for many days and nights, until they came to a place where there were great trees that were so big and so thick that even from a distance they seemed to almost touch the sky.

Suddenly they heard a strange noise near the water's edge. One of the young men picked up a rock to throw at the source of the noise. Suddenly, a great number of small, bright objects flew in the air.  The two young men were very frightened and ran back to their village, telling everyone they met about the strange objects falling from the sky.

The chief of the village decided to investigate. He took a group of strong young men and went to the place where the young men had seen the strange objects. When they arrived, they saw that it was not seals that the young men had heard but the sound of the rocks falling into the water. The chief and his group gathered up the strange objects. They were not rocks, but pieces of a bright metal.

The chief called for the village blacksmith to come and look at the metal. The blacksmith told the chief that it was silver and that they were very lucky to have found it. The chief decided to build a great house for himself and his family using the silver.

Later, a trader came to the village. When the chief told the trader how they had found the silver, the trader laughed and told the chief that it was his silver and that they had stolen it. The chief was very upset when he heard this. He and the trader argued for many days.

Finally, the chief decided to go to the Great House at L'kwungen to settle the argument. The chief explained the situation to the council of chiefs. The council decided that since the silver had been found and used to build a good house, it was rightfully the property of the chief and his people. The trader was very angry and decided to leave and never return.

The people of Egulac were very happy and grateful that they had found the silver. They continued to live in the house made of silver and enjoyed a prosperous life.

The story of Egulac's silver is a story of luck and of how the people of Egulac were able to keep what they considered to be rightfully theirs. It is also a story of how the people were able to use their resources, in this case the silver, to build a good and prosperous life for themselves and their families.

The men from Egulac were amazed at the success of the hunt and asked the two young men where they had learned to hunt seals so well. They told them that they had learned from their ancestors who lived long ago. They had learned that seals have a special place where they lose their strength and are easily killed. The men from Egulac were impressed by this knowledge and asked the two young men to teach them. Suddenly they heard a strange noise. One of them said it was a sea monster. But the other said it was a new kind of engine. They argued about it but could not decide. Just then an old man appeared and said it was both. He explained that there was a new kind of engine that ran on water and that was what they were hearing. The young men were amazed and asked where they could get such an engine. The old man told them to go to the north and they would find what they were looking for. So the young men set out on a long journey to find this new kind of engine.

The journey
They travelled for many days and met many strange people. They saw things they had never seen before and things that seemed impossible. But they finally came to a large city where they saw many strange machines. In one place they saw a machine that was pulling a large boat over the land. They asked about it and were told that it was a Land Ship. They also saw other strange machines that they could not figure out.

The engine
But in another place they saw a machine that looked like a large canoe with wings. The people there told them that it was a Water-Engine. They were amazed and asked where they could get one. The people told them that only the chief of the city had the power to give them a Water-Engine. So the young men went to the chief and told him about the noise they had heard by the river. The chief thought for a long time and then told them that they could have a Water-Engine. He gave them a small one because they were young and inexperienced.

The return
The young men were very happy and started back to Egulac right away. They were so excited that they did not notice the large storm that was coming. The waves were so high that they could hardly see. One wave hit them and they lost their Water-Engine. They looked for it but it was gone. They were very sad.

The test
When they finally got back to Egulac they told everyone about the Water-Engine. Some people did not believe them but others were impressed. They decided to test it to see if it was really a Water-Engine. They filled a large bowl with water and put the engine in it. They pulled on the ropes and sure enough the engine began to move. They were very excited

They heard a strange cry. One of them said it was the cry of a seal but the other said it was the cry of a human being in distress. They argued about it but decided to investigate. They went towards the cry and soon came upon a group of Indigenous people who were in a canoe. The people in the canoe were glad to see the two young men and invited them to join them. They gave the young men some fish and then told them a story. They said that long ago, before the white people came, there was a great flood. The people in the canoe were the only ones who had survived. They had been out in the boat for many days and were very hungry. They had heard the cries of the other people who were on the land but they could not go to them because the water had covered the land. They had cried out for help but no one had come. They were very glad when the two young men came along. The two young men were very impressed by this story and grateful for the food the other Indigenous people had given them. They decided to go back to their own people and tell them the story of the great flood. From then on, the two young men and the people in the canoe worked together and helped each other whenever they could.

Suddenly they heard a loud cry which seemed to come from the water itself. They were frightened and just as suddenly the sound was repeated on the other side of them. They looked out in the fog and saw two glowing lights approaching them. They were so close that the young men could see that the lights belonged to two big canoes coming towards them. The men could hear the paddlers breathing in the fog. Then the paddlers spoke in a language that the young men did not understand. The men were afraid and tried to paddle away but the canoes came closer still. Then the paddlers lit a fire and the men saw that they were not going to be attacked. Instead, the Tlingit Indians offered to trade. The young men traded their food and supplies for furs and other trade items they needed. The Tlingit Indians then paddled away into the fog.
The two young men returned home and told their people about the strange encounter. Their people were not surprised. They had heard stories of the Tlingit Indians who lived further up the coast. The people decided that they should go to these Tlingit people and trade with them for furs and other items they needed. So, the entire village made preparations to move. They built larger canoes that could carry more people and supplies. They took all their possessions and moved up the coast to the land of the Tlingit Indians. They traded with the Tlingit people and were able to get a large supply of furs and other items. They then returned to their homeland and told other villages about the trade they had made. This is how the Tlingit people became an important part of the Northwest Coast trade network.

They heard a strange noise and then saw two lights approaching them across the water. They thought it might be a couple of fishermen coming to join them, but as the lights came closer they could see that it was not fishermen but two large sea monsters with scary faces and long sharp teeth. The men were terrified and tried to paddle away as fast as they could, but the monsters overturned their canoe and dragged them under the water.

The next morning the bodies of the two young men were found on the shore and everyone was shocked and saddened by this tragic loss of life. The old people were called to the scene and they identified the bodies but they did not want to take them away for burial without first performing a ceremony to protect the people from the anger of the spirits of the two young men who had been killed by the sea monsters.

The ceremony lasted for several days and involved singing and dancing and offerings of food and tobacco. The people were afraid that if they did not do this the spirits of the two young men would take their anger out on the entire village. After the ceremony was finished the bodies were taken away for burial and everyone went back to their homes feeling relieved that the danger had passed.

But not everyone was happy. The two young men who had gone out in the canoe were brothers and the younger brother had been engaged to be married to a young woman in the village. Now he was dead and she was free to marry someone else. But she did not want to and the two young men who had been her fiancé's friends and had gone out in the canoe with him began to feel the full force of her anger. Suddenly they heard a strange noise, like the sound of a woman crying.  They looked around but could see nothing.  Suddenly, the cries came again, closer this time.  They looked in the water and saw a light on the water.  Then the cries came from that place and a woman's body floated up.  It was a spirit, come to warn them of danger.
The two young men were very frightened and tried to get away, but the spirit followed them and kept crying.  They ran to the village and told the people what had happened.  The old people knew that the woman was a spirit and that her crying was a warning of danger.  They decided to go back to the place where the young men had seen the light on the water.  They found a canoe that had been hidden there and took it out into the open water.  Then they saw a great light in the sky and knew that the danger was coming.  They rowed as fast as they could but the light caught them and they were all drowned.  The two young men went back to the village and told what had happened.  The old people made a feast and then held a potlatch to transfer their property to the spirit world.

They heard ominous sounds and saw strange lights.  They were afraid and decided to leave.  As they were walking up the hill to the right, they saw a strange being. It was a tall figure with a naked body, but it had four legs. It had a head with large eyes that shone brightly. It called out to them in a language they did not understand. They saw more of these beings around the hillside. They were terrified and ran back down to the canoes and went out on the water. Suddenly they heard a loud cry, and then another and another, and they knew that it was the cry of a human being and that it was coming from the water.  They could hear it distinctly, but they could not tell what it meant.  They waited and listened, and then they heard it again, and this time there was no mistaking it.  It was a cry for help.

The two young men were filled with fear, for they knew that no one could live near the water and survive the winter, and here were people crying for help in the fog and the darkness.  But they were brave, and they decided to try to save the people.  They went out into the water, calling to one another in low voices, and they followed the cry, and it led them to a place where they found three men who were almost frozen to death.  The young men brought them home to Egulac, and the next day they went back to the place where they had heard the cry, and they found three more men who were also lost in the cold.  They brought them home too, and when the old people of Egulac asked where they had found them, they said that they had been found near the water, but that there were more men out there who were still lost and crying.

The old people decided that they must go out and find the men, and they went out in canoes and searched for a long time, but they could not find any more men, only more cries in the fog and the darkness.  They searched and searched, but they could not find any more lost men, and they came home to Egulac wondering what had happened and wondering if they would ever know.  But the three men they had saved were grateful, and they stayed with the people of Egulac and learned their ways, and they became their friends and their brothers.  And so the people of Egulac knew that there were other people living near the water, and they lived happily ever after.

This story is from the Tlingit people.

Suddenly they heard a whirring noise near the water's edge. They could hardly believe their eyes when they saw a large sea monster lying on the shore. It was a Kusiro, a monster beaver which only appeared in such weather. The two young men were terrified and ran back to their village, leaving the Kusiro behind it.

The next day, they went back to the place where they had seen the monster, but it was gone. They were very disappointed. However, they continued to hunt seals every night in that place, and for several nights they saw the Kusiro. They were so excited that they forgot about the danger and tried to catch it. But the Kusiro was very fast and could slip away underwater. Eventually, the young men managed to catch it by using a large net. They were so proud of their victory that they decided to bring the Kusiro back to their village. But when they tried to lift the struggling monster onto their canoe, it slipped off the side and swam away. They tried several times but could not catch it. Finally, they gave up and went home.

The following day, the two young men went to the place where they had seen the Kusiro, but it was not there. They searched everywhere for it, but it was gone. They were very sad because they had lost their chance to bring the monster beaver back to their village.

Just then, an old woman appeared. She asked them why they looked so sad. They told her about the Kusiro and how they had tried to catch it but failed. The old woman smiled and said that they would never be able to catch the Kusiro because it was a spirit animal that only appeared to special people. She told them that they should be happy that they had seen it and that they should respect all the creatures in the water and on the land. The young men felt much better after talking to the old woman. From then on, they lived in harmony with the creatures of the water and the land.

Suddenly they heard a strange noise near the shore. It was a sound they had never heard before. It was low and guttural, like a bear grunting, but it was coming from the water. They were grateful for the knowledge the old people had given them. From then on they paid more attention to the old people and what they had to say. Suddenly they heard a strange noise near the water's edge. They called out and asked the owner of the voice to come out onto the beach. An old woman stepped forth, clad in furs and carrying a club. She explained that she was a powerful witch who had been sent by the Great Spirit to protect the salmon in the river. She promised to make the two young men rich if they would help her. The men agreed and the old woman then told them to go to the chief of the neighbouring tribe and steal his daughter. The young men were afraid but the old woman reassured them, saying that the girl would marry them willingly. The young men went to the chief's house and abducted the girl. When the old woman told them to, they buried the girl up to her neck in a mound of sand and left her there.

Soon after this, the two men caught a huge salmon which they took back to the old woman. She told them to cut the fish in two and take one half home with them. They did so and when they reached their village they opened their bundle to eat the salmon. However, as soon as they had taken a bite, the salmon vanished. They looked around for the old woman but she had disappeared too. They went back to the river and asked for her help again and again but she never appeared. The young men were now rich and lived off the salmon they caught for the rest of their lives.

This story is similar to other tales from around the world where a witch or magical being helps people to catch fish, such as the story of the Salmon of Knowledge from Irish mythology.
